```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)
```

## Problem 1

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

has_shared_birthday <- function(group_size) {
  birthdays <- sample(1:365, size = group_size, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}
```

```{r}
simulation_results <- expand.grid(
  group_size = 2:50,
  simulation = seq_len(10000)
)

simulation_results$shared_birthday <- vapply(
  simulation_results$group_size,
  has_shared_birthday,
  logical(1)
)

birthday_probabilities <- aggregate(
  shared_birthday ~ group_size,
  data = simulation_results,
  FUN = mean
)
```

```{r}
ggplot(birthday_probabilities, aes(x = group_size, y = shared_birthday)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of at least one shared birthday",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Estimated probability"
  )
```

The estimated probability rises as the group gets larger. The increase is steepest at moderate group sizes, then slows as the probability approaches 1. This happens because there are many possible pairs of people that could match: adding people creates more opportunities for a shared birthday.

## Problem 2

After downloading `hw5_data.zip` from the assignment link and uncompressing it
into a folder named `data` in this homework directory, the code below reads
each participant's file. The filenames encode the study arm and subject ID
(for example, `con_1.csv` and `exp_1.csv`).

```{r}
files <- list.files("./data", full.names = TRUE)

participants <- files %>%
  set_names(basename(files)) %>%
  map(~ read_csv(.x, show_col_types = FALSE)) %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "file_name") %>%
  mutate(file_name = sub("\\.csv$", "", file_name)) %>%
  separate_wider_delim(
    file_name,
    delim = "_",
    names = c("arm", "participant_id")
  )

data <- participants %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) %>%
  mutate(week = parse_number(week))
```


```{r}
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(x = week, y = observation, group = participant_id, color = participant_id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = .6) +
  facet_grid(. ~ arm) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly observations by study arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation"
  ) +
  guides(color = "none")
```
The spaghetti plot shows each participant's measurements over time in
separate panels for the control and experimental arms. The experimental group
generally shows an upward trajectory over time, while the control group is
comparatively stable. Individual trajectories vary within each group, but the
overall pattern suggests that observed value in participants increased more in the experimental arm.

## Problem 3
```{r}
set.seed(1000)

power_simulation <- expand_grid(
  true_mean = 0:6,
  simulation = seq_len(5000)
) %>%
  mutate(
    test_results = map(true_mean, function(mu) {
      sample_data <- rnorm(n = 30, mean = mu, sd = 5)
      broom::tidy(t.test(sample_data, mu = 0))
    })
  ) %>%
  unnest(test_results) %>%
  mutate(reject_null = p.value < 0.05)

power_summary <- power_simulation %>%
  group_by(true_mean) %>%
  summarize(
    power = mean(reject_null),
    mean_estimate = mean(estimate),
    mean_estimate_when_rejected = mean(estimate[reject_null]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

power_summary
```

```{r}
ggplot(power_summary, aes(x = true_mean, y = power)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Power of a one-sample t-test",
    x = "True population mean",
    y = "Proportion of tests rejecting the null (Power)"
  )
```
Power increases with the difference between the true mean and
the null value of 0. When the true mean is 0, the rejection proportion should
be near the 5% significance level. As the true mean moves away from 0, the
test more often detects the difference and power approaches 100%.

```{r}
estimate_summary <- power_summary %>%
  select(true_mean, mean_estimate, mean_estimate_when_rejected) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_estimate, mean_estimate_when_rejected),
    names_to = "estimate_type",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    estimate_type = recode(
      estimate_type,
      mean_estimate = "All samples",
      mean_estimate_when_rejected = "Null rejected"
    )
  )

ggplot(estimate_summary, aes(x = true_mean, y = average_estimate,
                             color = estimate_type, linetype = estimate_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Average estimated mean by true mean",
    x = "True population mean",
    y = "Average estimated mean",
    color = "Samples",
    linetype = "Samples"
  ) 
```
Across all samples, the average estimate should be close to the true mean,
because the sample mean is an unbiased estimator. Among only the samples that
reject the null, the average estimate is generally farther from 0, especially
for small nonzero true means. This happens because selection on a significant
result favors samples whose estimates happened to fall far enough from 0 to
cross the significance threshold. Therefore, the average estimate in
significant samples is not generally equal to the true mean.
